title: Client portal admin token published by a contractor at an accounting firm
summary: A client phones to ask who downloaded their tax documents overnight, and the portal vendor warns of an overage charge for unusual download volume. A freelance developer hired to connect the portal to the practice-management system had posted a working administrator token in a public code repository. With no IT staff, a filing deadline five days away and a log that reaches back only 30 days, the exercise tests who takes charge, who can shut off access, and when clients and the insurer are told.

setting.company_profile: A 25-person accounting firm with no servers and no IT staff: it runs on Microsoft 365, a client document portal and a practice-management system, with an outside IT provider looking after laptops and email. It carries cyber insurance and promises confidentiality and breach notice in its client engagement letters.
setting.day_and_time: Wednesday, 9:20 a.m., five days before the personal tax filing deadline
setting.initial_signal: A long-standing client phones the managing partner: the client document portal emailed them a receipt saying their tax documents were downloaded at 2:14 a.m., and nobody in their household did it. The same morning the portal vendor emails the office manager that the account has used 40 times its normal download volume and an overage charge is coming.

roles.name: Incident Commander
roles.responsibilities: Takes charge as soon as the client's call and the vendor's notice are connected, with a partner's authority to spend money and to switch off portal integrations during deadline week.

roles.name: Technical Lead
roles.responsibilities: Works with the portal vendor's support desk and the outside IT provider to revoke tokens, remove the developer's access and obtain the audit log.

roles.name: Communications Lead
roles.responsibilities: Speaks for the company to clients, starting with the one who phoned, and gives staff one script so that nobody improvises an answer.

roles.name: Legal and Compliance Lead
roles.responsibilities: Calls the cyber insurer's breach hotline, works with the breach lawyer and tracks the notice promised to clients in the engagement letters.

roles.name: Scribe
roles.responsibilities: Keeps a dated record of every call, finding and decision, including who approved outside spending and when the insurer was told.

objectives: Name the person who takes charge of an incident in a company with no IT staff, and a backup for when that person is with a client.
Confirm that at least two people can sign in to the client portal as administrators and revoke an API token within the hour.
Decide when the cyber insurer is called and who may approve outside spending before that call.
Decide what clients are told, by whom and by when, while the list of affected folders is still incomplete.
Produce a list of every outside person or company with access to client data, and who approved each one.

injects.title: A client asks who downloaded their tax documents
injects.narrative: Wednesday, 9:20 a.m. A long-standing client phones the managing partner. The client document portal emailed them a receipt saying their tax documents were downloaded at 2:14 a.m., and nobody in their household did it. The managing partner promises to look into it and goes into a meeting. Separately, the office manager has an email from the portal vendor: the account has used 40 times its normal download volume this month, and a $1,900 overage charge will be added to the next invoice. The office manager assumes it is a billing mistake. The outside IT provider looks after laptops and Microsoft 365; the portal is not in its contract. Nobody has connected the two messages yet, and there is no IT person on staff to hand them to.
questions: Who takes charge the moment these two messages are connected, and who is the backup if that person is with a client?
Who is called first, the portal vendor, the IT provider or the cyber insurer, and who makes each call?
What does the managing partner tell the client who phoned, today, before anything is confirmed?
expected_actions: Pull the managing partner out of the meeting and name an Incident Commander who can make decisions and approve spending today.
The office manager opens an urgent ticket with the portal vendor's support desk asking which login or token made the 2:14 a.m. download.
Keep the client's receipt email and the vendor's notice, and write down the time each one arrived.

injects.title: Three tokens, one administrator and deadline week
injects.narrative: The portal vendor's support desk replies within the hour. The downloads were made with an API token, a password that lets another program sign in to the portal. It is named 'integration-test', has full administrator rights and was created five weeks ago from the office manager's login. The admin page lists three tokens: that one, one used for e-signatures, and one nobody recognizes. The office manager is the portal's only administrator and is not sure which token does what. Revoking all three would stop the downloads, but might also break e-signatures and the nightly sync to the practice-management system in the busiest week of the year. The IT provider offers to help at its emergency rate of $250 an hour, which needs a partner's approval.
questions: Who decides whether to revoke all three tokens now and accept that e-signatures and the nightly sync may stop during deadline week?
If the office manager were away today, who else could sign in to the portal as an administrator?
Who can approve the IT provider's emergency rate, and should that wait until the insurer has been called?
expected_actions: Export the portal's audit log, its record of who downloaded what, and screenshot the token list with creation dates before changing anything.
The office manager revokes the 'integration-test' token and the unrecognized token in the portal's admin settings, then tests an e-signature and the nightly sync.
Ask the vendor's support desk to confirm in writing which token each integration uses, and tell staff in Microsoft Teams what may be interrupted.

injects.title: The developer's account does not match the log
injects.narrative: The office manager remembers the token. Six weeks ago the company hired a freelance developer, recommended by a client, to connect the portal to the practice-management system. There is no signed contract, only emails. Reached by email, the developer explains that the working script, with the token inside it, was posted in a public repository on a personal GitHub account as a portfolio sample. The developer says it was public for two days at most and was switched to private last night after another developer pointed out the token. The portal's audit log says otherwise: the token was used from unfamiliar locations on nine separate days. The developer still has a guest account in the company's Microsoft 365 and a login to the practice-management system, and offers to help investigate.
questions: Which does the company act on, the developer's two days or the log's nine, and who decides?
Who removes the developer's Microsoft 365 guest account and practice-management login, and does that happen before or after accepting the offer of help?
Who is the one person who speaks to the developer from now on, and what is the developer asked to keep and hand over?
expected_actions: The IT provider blocks the developer's guest account in the Microsoft 365 admin center and the office manager disables the practice-management login, both today.
Send the developer a written request to keep the script, the repository and all messages about the project, and to delete nothing.
Record nine days as the minimum exposure, and check the practice-management system's login history for the developer's account.

injects.title: The log goes back 30 days; the token is 35 days old
injects.narrative: By mid-afternoon the audit log export is in. Over nine days the token downloaded 1,140 files from 212 of the company's 380 client folders: tax returns, wage statements, bank statements and scans of identity documents. Few clients have download receipts switched on, which is why only one has called. On the company's subscription the log goes back only 30 days, and the token existed for 35. The vendor can retrieve older records, but only on a written request from the account owner, and that takes three to five business days. One partner argues that only the 212 clients need to hear anything. Another points out that the token could open every folder, including payroll files holding the bank details of clients' employees. Staff are asking whether to keep using the portal this week.
questions: While five days of history are missing, does the company treat 212 folders or all 380 as exposed, and who makes that call?
Who is the account owner who signs the request for older records today, and who chases the vendor until they arrive?
Do staff keep using the portal for this week's filings, and who tells them?
expected_actions: The account owner sends the vendor the written request for the older audit records today and asks for it to be expedited.
Build one spreadsheet of the 212 confirmed folders with client name, types of file downloaded and the partner responsible, and mark the other 168 as unknown.
Tell staff in writing by the end of the day whether the portal stays in use, and name the one person who answers client questions.

injects.title: The insurer, the engagement letter and costs already run up
injects.narrative: Thursday, 11:30 a.m. The cyber insurance policy is on the table. It requires notice to the insurer's breach hotline as soon as practicable, and says costs run up before notice, without the insurer's consent, may not be covered. That could include any emergency hours the IT provider worked before the call. The hotline assigns a breach lawyer and asks two things: when did the company first know, and does it still review outside access to client data every quarter, as it answered on last year's questionnaire? Nobody reviewed the developer's access. Meanwhile the standard engagement letter promises clients notice within three business days of discovering unauthorized access to their information. That runs out on Monday morning, deadline day, and the lawyer cannot review a client notice until tomorrow.
questions: At what point should the insurer have been called, by whom, and who approved the IT provider's hours before that call?
The engagement letter's three business days run out on Monday morning: who decides whether clients get a short notice before the full facts are known?
Who answers the insurer's question about the quarterly access review, and what is the accurate answer?
expected_actions: Give the hotline the facts as they stand: first client call on Wednesday at 9:20 a.m., tokens revoked, 212 folders confirmed, five days of log missing.
Send the breach lawyer the engagement letter wording and the Monday deadline, and book the review of the client notice for Friday.
Ask the lawyer which state breach-notice laws and tax-agency reporting duties apply, and put each deadline and owner on one list.

injects.title: The stolen files are being used, and staff are improvising
injects.narrative: Thursday, 3:30 p.m. A second client forwards an email that appears to come from the company. It quotes the exact refund from last year's return and asks the client to confirm bank details for this year's. It was not sent from the company's Microsoft 365. Someone is already using the downloaded files against clients. Meanwhile a staff accountant, trying to help, has emailed three worried clients that there was a small technical issue and nothing to worry about. The lawyer's reviewed notice will not be ready until tomorrow afternoon, and two partners want to wait for it. A third partner wants a warning about fake emails sent to all 380 clients tonight. With the filing deadline four days away, clients are asking whether to send their documents by email instead.
questions: Who decides whether a warning about fake emails goes to all 380 clients tonight, ahead of the full notice, and who approves the wording?
Who corrects what the three clients were told, and how does the company stop staff answering on their own?
How do clients send documents safely over the next four days, and who tells them?
expected_actions: Send every client a short warning tonight, cleared with the breach lawyer by phone: the company never asks for bank details by email, and here is the number to call.
The Communications Lead phones the three clients who were told nothing was wrong and gives them the accurate position.
Give staff a one-paragraph script and a single contact for client questions, and have the IT provider block the fake sender's address in Microsoft 365.

wrap_up_questions: When did the group know exactly who decides, and when did everyone wait for someone else?
What was missing: a named person in charge, a second portal administrator, a signed contract with the developer, longer log history, or the insurer's hotline number?
Which parts of the plan, the portal's settings and the way outside developers are hired get rewritten, and by when?
Which partner owns each of those changes, and who checks they are done before the next insurance renewal?
